title: Responsible AI Is Not Universal
section: I keep coming back to the word “responsible”
text:
I keep coming back to the word “responsible”
When we say or call for use of artificial intelligence in a responsible way, what exactly do we mean?.
It is one of those words that has become almost impossible to escape when lost in the labyrinths of technical discourse. Responsible AI. Trustworthy AI. Ethical AI. Human-centered AI. We have developed principles around fairness, transparency, accountability, privacy, safety, and human oversight. Governments are writing strategies around them. Companies are building governance programs around them. Researchers are developing increasingly sophisticated ways of evaluating whether AI systems meet them.
All of this work are important. But the more I read about it, the more I keep asking: responsible according to whom, and responsible under what conditions?
Artificial intelligence governance, and truthfully, a huge chunk of technological endeavours is often discussed through the lens of Western technological and regulatory centers. This essay front-lines the argument that many of today’s governance frameworks look past the social, political, and technological realities of the Global South, and that these regions should have a rather active role in shaping the future of responsible AI.
To be clear, I do not mean that there should be one form of responsible AI for Europe, another for Africa, and another for Latin America. Because, human rights do not become negotiable all of a sudden when we cross a border. So, neither should concerns about discrimination, exploitation, safety, or accountability.
What I am questioning is the assumption that we can decide what responsible AI looks like in a small number of powerful technological and regulatory centers and then export that understanding elsewhere. That is a very different proposition.

title: Responsible AI Is Not Universal
text:
Governance always comes from somewhere
No governance framework appears from nowhere. They come mostly from particular institutions, histories, political systems, technological capabilities, economic priorities, and understandings of risk. Even the problems that are eventually problematic enough to warrant our beloved governable attention are shaped by these conditions.
Think about some of the frameworks that now structure global conversations about AI.
The UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence was adopted in 2021 and remains one of the most ambitious attempts to articulate a genuinely global approach to AI ethics. It centers human rights and dignity and identifies principles including fairness, transparency, human oversight, environmental sustainability, diversity, and inclusion. Importantly, it also goes beyond abstract principles to recommend action in areas like data governance, education, health, gender, culture, and international cooperation.
This recognizes something that can very well easily disappear in technical conversations about AI. Because these systems enter societies, they interact with institutions that already exist, inequalities that already exist, languages that already exist, and histories that certainly did not begin with artificial intelligence. Still, international agreement on principles does not cancel out differences in the conditions under which those principles have to become material.
Technical transparency means little when the institutions expected to demand it lack the technical capacity to. Privacy protections mean something different where large portions of the population are only beginning to enter formal digital infrastructures (think of the challenges in sub-Saharan Africa). Human oversight assumes not just the presence of a human being, but people with the authority, knowledge, resources, and institutional support to intervene. This is where and why I think our conversations about responsible AI sometimes become too neat, ignoring conditions requires to activate them. All I am saying is that these principles travel much more easily than the conditions required to implement them.

title: Responsible AI Is Not Universal
section: The Global South is not an empty space waiting for governance
text:
The Global South is not an empty space waiting for governance
There is yet another assumption that bothers me. Discussions about AI governance in the Global South sometimes make these regions sound like places waiting for governance to arrive. The language gives it away. capacity building, technology transfer, regulatory readiness, adoption, catching up.
Some of these are legitimate concerns because infrastructure are truly needed, technical capacity is required, investment is necessary. But the framing of these concepts tend to establish a hierarchy in which some parts of the world produce technology, standards, and knowledge while others receive them.
Shakir Mohamed, Marie-Therese Png, and William Isaac challenged this relationship directly in their 2020 paper, “Decolonial AI: Decolonial Theory as Sociotechnical Foresight in Artificial Intelligence”. Their argument provides impetus for us to examine how histories of power continue to shape which knowledge matter more, who participates in technological development, and who bears its consequences. They propose, among other things, critical technical practice and what they call “reverse tutelage”: creating conditions in which communities usually positioned as recipients of technological knowledge become sources from whom technologists must learn.
Importantly, this allows us to move beyond asking How do we bring responsible AI to the Global South? to asking What could the rest of the world learn about responsible AI from the Global South?

title: Responsible AI Is Not Universal
section: Technology travels. Context does not travel with it.
text:
Technology travels. Context does not travel with it.
AI systems can cross borders almost instantly, but the social worlds into which they arrive do not. A model developed primarily using English-language data can be deployed in a country containing hundreds of languages. So is an automated decision system developed within one administrative tradition which then enter another where documentation, institutional capacity, or relationships between citizens and the state are fundamentally different. A governance framework built around individual privacy can encounter communities where understandings of data, identity, responsibility, and social harm are not exclusively individual.
These are not peripheral implementation problems, for they affect whether a system can be considered responsible ab initio. The work of Masakhane offers a concrete example from African natural language processing. The researchers began from an obvious but consequential imbalance, that Africa contains more than 2,000 languages, yet African languages have historically accounted for only a small fraction of NLP resources and research. Instead of waiting for better representation to emerge from the dominant centers of machine learning, Masakhane built a distributed, continent-wide research community around African machine translation.
There is something larger than machine translation here. Masakhane shows what changes when people closest to a technological problem are not just consulted after systems have been designed but participate in defining the problem, building the infrastructure, producing the knowledge, and determining what progress should look like. That, to me, is also a governance question.

title: Responsible AI Is Not Universal
text:
Data has a geography too
The same problem becomes even more complicated when we think about data. AI systems do not just use data. They depend on enormous infrastructures for collecting, classifying, storing, transferring, and monetizing it. Nick Couldry and Ulises Mejias describe this broader process as data colonialism in The Costs of Connection. Their argument connects contemporary data extraction to much older histories of appropriation. The resource being captured has changed, but questions about who extracts value, who controls infrastructure, and who gets to determine the terms of participation are ultimately the same.
Thinking about AI globally. Where are the data coming from? Where are they processed? Where are the models trained? Where are the profits captured? Where are the harms experienced? Who owns the infrastructure? Whose languages are training data? Whose creative work are training material? Where are data centers located? Who receives the economic value produced from these resources? And when something goes wrong, which institutions actually have enough power to demand an answer?
Responsible AI cannot only concern what a model does at the moment someone interacts with it. Responsibility also has to extend backward into the infrastructures and relationships that made the model possible. Otherwise, there is a risk of governing the visible system while leaving the political economy underneath it largely untouched.

title: Responsible AI Is Not Universal
section: Africa is already writing its own AI future
text:
Africa is already writing its own AI future
This is also why I think it is becoming inaccurate to describe African countries just as recipients of global AI governance. In 2024, the African Union endorsed its Continental Artificial Intelligence Strategy. The strategy explicitly describes its approach as Africa-centric and development-focused, connecting AI to Agenda 2063 and priorities including education, healthcare, agriculture, innovation, employment, cultural preservation, infrastructure, and economic development.
This is significant given that the ordering of priorities is not identical to what is obtained in every Western AI policy conversation. And why should it be? A society thinking about frontier-model catastrophic risk, another thinking about automating an already highly digitized labor market, and another thinking about whether AI could expand access to healthcare in areas with severe physician shortages are all discussing AI risk. But they are not necessarily discussing the same configuration of risks.
Development too can be an AI governance concern. So can linguistic inclusion, technological dependency, access to compute, the concentration of AI infrastructure outside the continent, the ability of local researchers to build rather than perpetually consume.
The challenge is not to replace safety with development or rights with innovation. It is to resist the idea that the hierarchy of AI problems established elsewhere must automatically become the hierarchy of AI problems everywhere.

title: Responsible AI Is Not Universal
section: I am also uncomfortable with the word “localization”
text:
I am also uncomfortable with the word “localization”
Even localization, a word I have used myself, steadily seem to be insufficient.
Localization can imply that the important intellectual work has already happened. Meaning that someone develops the framework, and someone else adapts it. Or probably change a few provisions, add local examples, translate the document, consult some stakeholders, and now it is localized.
But what if the starting assumptions need to change? The Decolonial AI Manyfesto pushes this question further by challenging both the actors who has the power to define, build, and govern AI, as well as the language through which AI is imagined. It asks us to recognize artificial intelligence as more than a technical object, to look at it as a knowledge system, a collection of narratives and relationships, and an imaginary about what kinds of futures are possible.
The significance of this is that governance does not restrict technology, it tells us what technology is for. It makes provisions about what should be optimized, which harms deserve intervention, which benefits justify risk, whose knowledge counts as source, and which futures are worth investing in. These are first political and social questions before they are technical ones.

title: Responsible AI Is Not Universal
section: Representation is not the same as power
text:
Representation is not the same as power
Of course, the obvious response is that global AI governance is becoming more inclusive. And it is. Do not get me wrong. In fact, there are more conversations about the Global South. More international organizations are emphasizing geographic representation. African governments are developing national AI strategies. Researchers from historically underrepresented regions are increasingly visible in global AI debates. This is progress.
But I think we need to differentiate between being represented in a conversation and having the power to structure the conversation. This is like inviting someone to a meeting after the agenda has already been written, or like making a decision and then asking for feedback on it. It is not the same as having the power to set the agenda, define the problems, and determine what the appropriate solution should be. That is what adding researchers from the Global South to a governance initiative whose fundamental assumptions about risk, development, infrastructure, and responsibility have already been decided does.
While all of those things technically are forms of participation, but they do not necessarily redistribute power. Therefore, the question of responsible AI cannot end with representation. It has to include agenda-setting. Setting agendas that allow these regions to define what responsible AI means in their own contexts. To ask questions like: Who gets to decide what the important AI problems are? Who defines the categories through which those problems are measured? Who writes the standards? Who owns the infrastructure needed to comply with those standards? Who can afford compliance? And who is described as irresponsible when they cannot?
These questions become particularly important as governance frameworks steadily move from voluntary principles toward standards, audits, evaluations, and legal requirements.

title: Responsible AI Is Not Universal
section: Maybe universality should be the destination, not the starting point
text:
Maybe universality should be the destination, not the starting point
I am not arguing against global AI governance, quite the opposite. Artificial intelligence is too interconnected for purely national approaches to be sufficient. Models, data, companies, workers, and harms cross borders. There are good reasons to develop shared standards around human rights, safety, accountability, and dignity. But perhaps we have the process backward. Instead of beginning with a supposedly universal understanding of responsible AI and asking how the rest of the world can implement it, we might begin with different social realities and ask what principles can survive serious conversation among them.
Universality, then, would not mean that one framework successfully traveled everywhere. It would mean that something genuinely shared was produced through negotiation among different ways of understanding technology and society. That, I believe, is harder. It is also slower and more likely to produce disagreements. But, maybe, responsible AI should be difficult.

title: Responsible AI Is Not Universal
section: The Global South should not only be governed
text:
The Global South should not only be governed
The future of artificial intelligence will not belong exclusively to the countries currently building the largest models. AI systems will enter classrooms in Onitsha, hospitals in Nairobi, government offices in Delhi, farms in Brazil, newsrooms in Johannesburg, financial systems in Accra, and homes everywhere in between. People in these places will encounter possibilities that were not anticipated in Silicon Valley or Brussels. They will also encounter failures that existing evaluation frameworks may never have been designed to detect. So their experiences should not become case studies that we collect after deployment. They should become knowledge from which AI is governed ab initio.
So, a somewhat controversial stance in this piece is that the Global South does not need to reject ideas developed elsewhere just because they were developed elsewhere, nor should every difference be romanticized as local knowledge. Some principles deserve to travel, but they should not travel unexamined. They should be interrogated, tested, and adapted to the conditions in which they are deployed.
If responsible AI is actually going to mean something globally, then the regions in which AI is deployed must have the power to question its assumptions, redefine its risks, contribute their own knowledge, and shape the institutions that govern it.
The Global South should not just be where the future of AI arrives. It should be one of the places from which that future is imagined.

title: We’re building it. Do we know why?
text:
Back to Commentary
Today, some of the most powerful people in technology sat down for lunch at the White House and signed a pledge. Trump called it “morally binding,” almost like a constitution. The White House billed the event as a meeting and luncheon on Super Intelligence, and Trump said the technology has now been officially renamed SI.
The renaming got my attention first. I wasn’t exactly sure why that took national priority at a time of heightened international tensions. But perhaps that was exactly the point. To lead, to be first, or to dominate the international race for technological supremacy. Naming it was itself a way of claiming the lead, even before anyone had clearly explained what we were racing toward or why it was worth getting there. I. J. Good imagined an “ultraintelligent machine” back in 1965, one that could design better machines and would be the last invention we’d ever need to make. Bostrom later defined superintelligence in Superintelligence as an intellect that greatly exceeds ours in practically every domain. Nobody at that table could tell you how we’d recognize the day it finally arrives, if at all. But a name does a lot. Calling a technology “superintelligence” tells people to lean in and stop asking questions.

title: We’re building it. Do we know why?
text:
Why do we want it?
The answer you hear most is that it will cure disease and end scarcity. Some people mean that sincerely. The answer you can actually see in the room is different. Trump said whoever wins superintelligence wins. He also argued the government can’t slow development for fear of falling behind China.
That’s a race, and a race isn’t a purpose. Scott Alexander’s essay “Meditations on Moloch” describes the trap where everyone would prefer a slower, safer pace, but no one can afford to slow down alone, so everyone speeds up. Zuckerberg has pushed back on calls to slow down collectively, arguing that every lab has the incentive to move at the pace needed to train models safely. But look at whose pace that is. It’s set by the competition, not by anyone’s judgment about what’s wise.
Rich Sutton’s “Bitter Lesson” explains why the race appears to be so rational. Over seventy years, general methods that scale with compute have beaten clever human-designed ones. So the bet is simple: keep scaling and the capability arrives. What the bet leaves out is for what. We’re arguing about how much intelligence is coming and skipping the question of what it should want.
That question is the philosophical center of all this. Bostrom’s orthogonality thesis says how smart a system is and what it wants are separate questions. It is Hume’s is-ought gap in a new outfit, because nothing about being good at achieving goals tells you which goals is worth achieving. The comforting intuition, that a wise enough mind would naturally be a kind one, has no backing. Stuart Russell makes the practical version of the point in Human Compatible. The standard model of AI, where we specify an objective and the machine optimizes it, is the problem. The failure is not that the machine disobeys, it is that it obeys perfectly.
The strangest feature of this moment is that the warnings come from inside the building. Dario Amodei published an essay this month, “We Must Pace the Frontier,” arguing for a cooperative slowdown, and it set off a fierce debate. People are telling us it may be dangerous, that they’re building it anyway, and that stopping isn’t an option. I honestly do not read that as hypocrisy. It’s what a coordination problem looks like from the inside.

title: We’re building it. Do we know why?
section: Who polices a mind we can’t read?
text:
Who polices a mind we can’t read?
Wittgenstein said in the Philosophical Investigations that if a lion could speak, we couldn’t understand him. Nagel asked “What Is It Like to Be a Bat?” and concluded we can’t really know. If we can’t cross that gap with a bat, the idea that we’ll oversee a mind that outthinks us across the board raises some eyebrows. Interpretability research is a serious attempt to close it, but it’s early.
Against that backdrop, the governance looks thin. A constitution binds power because something outside the powerful enforces it. Plainly, I mean courts, voters, institutions that can say no. The tech CEOs said they agreed on a safety accord, but it appeared to be voluntary. A promise you enforce on yourself is a good intention, and that isn’t worthless. It just isn’t a constitution.
There is a precedent for scientists policing themselves. In 1975, biologists met at Asilomar and set voluntary rules for recombinant DNA, and people still argue over whether that was wisdom or a way to head off regulation. Even so, a gene-splicing rule constrains a technique. Nobody knows yet what a rule constrains when the thing being governed can out-think the governors.
To be fair, there are smart skeptics. Yann LeCun argues that language models alone will get us nowhere near human-level reasoning and that we need new architectures that can plan and understand the world. He also says that fears of runaway systems wrongly equate intelligence with a drive to dominate. He might be right. I just notice that “he might be right” isn’t much comfort when the downside is this lopsided.

title: We’re building it. Do we know why?
section: What does it mean for us?
text:
What does it mean for us?
Hannah Arendt opened The Human Condition in 1958 with Sputnik and a fear that has aged strangely well. She feared a society of laborers about to be freed from labor, with nothing to replace it, having forgotten how to do anything else. Keynes had made a gentler version of the bet in 1930, in “Economic Possibilities for Our Grandchildren,” predicting his grandchildren would work fifteen hours a week and that the hard part would be learning how to live. We got the productivity without the leisure. If superintelligence delivers real abundance, the open question is still what people are for.
Hans Jonas put the stakes best in The Imperative of Responsibility: act so that the effects of your action are compatible with the permanence of genuine human life. He wrote it in 1979, about technology in general. It reads now as if it were written for this week.
I don’t think doom is certain, and I don’t think the optimists have earned their confidence either. What I do believe is that the engineering questions, real and important as they are, sit on top of a philosophical one we’ve dodged for a few thousand years: What do we value? What would we want a mind more capable than us to do? And can we say it, together, clearly enough to hand it to something that will take us literally? Today’s lunch produced a new name and a voluntary pledge. It didn’t answer that question, and I doubt anyone in the room would claim it did.

title: Amaka Peace Onebunne
text:
Hi! This is me…
I am a Ph.D. student in the Lew Klein College of Media and Communication at Temple University, where I study emerging technology as part of the social, communicative, and institutional systems through which people produce knowledge, make decisions, coordinate work, and understand the world around them.
My research is broadly sociotechnical and grounded in communication. I am interested in the relationships that form around AI systems, i.e. between people and machines, among people whose interactions are increasingly mediated by technology, between workers and organizations, between technical systems and institutional rules, and increasingly, among AI systems in the same social and information environments. I look at how these systems reshape relationships, professional roles, cultural practices, forms of expression, and the ways people understand themselves and others.
Some of my work examines these questions through journalism, organizations, and knowledge infrastructures. Other projects examine AI systems and governance frameworks across different social and institutional contexts, particularly in Africa and the Global South.

Federal Polytechnic Oko to Graduate Study
My academic journey began at Federal Polytechnic Oko, where I earned a Higher National Diploma in Mass Communication. I was trained in journalism, broadcasting, public communication, and media production.
During my master’s degree in Communication Studies at Northern Illinois University, I became especially interested in AI’s growing role in producing, interpreting, and communicating information. My master’s research was advised by Dr. Andrea L. Guzman, whose work in Human–Machine Communication gave me a way to think seriously about the changing relationships between people and intelligent machines.
For my thesis, Journalists’ Perception of Artificial Intelligence: The Case of Nigerian Newsrooms, I interviewed 18 news workers including reporters, editors, producers, fact-checkers etc about how AI was becoming part of their everyday work.
My interest was in the changes around AI use. These journalists talked about speed and creative assistance alongside verification, professional judgment, cultural accuracy, newsroom expectations, and systems that sometimes struggled with contexts they are familiar with. AI was entering an existing social and professional environment, where journalists had to decide when to trust it, when to question it, how to work around its limitations, and how much space it should occupy within their professional practice.
That study changed the kinds of questions I subsequently started asking about technology. But for the most part, journalism was where I first encountered many of these questions, and they have since expanded. Africa is key to how I think about these questions. Specifically, because many ideas about technological progress, adoption, risk, and responsibility spread in a supposedly universal manner. Focusing on African contexts gives me a place to examine those assumptions, and think about technological futures from contexts that have been mostly peripheral to their making.

title: Amaka Peace Onebunne
text:
Doctoral Research at Temple
I am now pursuing my Ph.D. under the guidance of Dr. Andrew Iliadis at Temple University’s Lew Klein College of Media and Communication.
My doctoral work expands many of the questions that first brought me to the study of technology and society.
Across my projects, I typically ask:

How do emerging technologies change the ways people communicate, produce knowledge, and make decisions?
How do people decide when to trust, question, resist, or rely on intelligent and automated systems?
What happens to professional judgment and expertise as more forms of work become mediated by machines?
How do relationships between people and machines change as technologies become more communicative and autonomous?
How are responsibility and risk distributed across people, organizations, institutions, and technical systems?
How do technologies carry particular assumptions about people, knowledge, and society into the environments where they are used?
What happens when technologies move across cultural, political, and institutional contexts?

I approach these questions in different ways depending on the problem.

title: Amaka Peace Onebunne
text:
Current Research
My research broadly examines the relationships among technology, people, knowledge, and institutions. Some of the questions I am currently working through include:

Human–machine judgment: I am developing work with synthetic users and persona-based evaluators to examine whether their judgments are stable and whether machines can meaningfully represent human experiences in evaluation.
Agentic systems and failure: I am studying how failures move through multi-agent AI systems, including how small failures become system-level problems and how coordination and redundancy might improve recovery.
Machines and knowledge: I am interested in the growing role of machines in producing, organizing, and evaluating knowledge. My current work examines how AI-generated information reenters the information environment and becomes part of later outputs, raising questions about sources, authority, and what we eventually accept as knowledge.
AI, journalism, and representation: My published and ongoing research examines journalists’ experiences with AI, deepfakes in African news coverage, and the role of algorithms in shaping how Africa is represented and made visible online.
Technological futures and the Global South: I study how governments, technology companies, and other institutions imagine the Global South within emerging technological futures, particularly through narratives of AI expansion, development, opportunity, and responsibility.
Risk, responsibility, and organizations: I examine how organizations define and communicate technological risk, who gets to decide that something is a problem, and where responsibility is placed when intelligent systems fail or cause harm.

Methods & Research Practice
My research combines computational, qualitative, and mixed methods, depending on the questions I am asking. I work with text and network analysis, statistical modeling, computational experiments, AI evaluation, interviews, and discourse analysis.
I primarily work in Python and R to build the datasets, code, and workflows my projects require, using tools like pandas, spaCy, scikit-learn, quanteda, Jupyter, Git, and GitHub. I also have experience with interviews, thematic analysis, discourse analysis, and human studies.

title: Amaka Peace Onebunne
text:
Beyond Research
Before beginning my Ph.D., I worked across journalism, communications, education, and corporate environments. These experiences still shape how I approach technology and the questions I ask.
Journalism taught me to think seriously about information, verification, trust, and the realities of working under institutional constraints. My experiences in communications, education, and corporate settings exposed me to very different ways that people coordinate, make decisions, share knowledge, and adapt to new technologies.
Having worked across these spaces also keeps me interested in the distance between how technologies are imagined and how they become part of everyday practice. People interpret them, work around them, resist them, depend on them, and sometimes use them in ways their designers never anticipated.

title: Amaka Peace Onebunne
text:
Where I Am Headed
I want to build a research career around understanding the changing relationships among people, technology, organizations, and knowledge. Artificial intelligence is a major part of that work today, alongside my general interest in emerging technologies and the social systems that develop around them.
I want my work to contribute to how we understand, evaluate, and live with increasingly intelligent technologies, especially as the boundaries between human and machine communication, knowledge, judgment, and action become harder to draw.

title: AI Risk Is a Communication Problem
section: I think we are looking at AI risk too late
text:
I think we are looking at AI risk too late
Systems surround much of the conversations when we talk about AI risk. We ask whether a model is accurate, biased, can be manipulated, hallucinates, whether private information is leaking, someone can jailbreak it, and whether it behaves safely under adversarial conditions.
These are quite frankly important concerns. I spend a great deal of time thinking about them myself. But of lately I have been wondering whether our understanding of AI risk starts too late. Because by the time we are asking whether a model is biased, hallucinating, or leaking private information, the system has already been deployed. It has already entered workplaces, hospitals, schools, government agencies, financial institutions, newsrooms, and homes. It has already produced outputs that someone has to interpret and act on. Someone trusted information they should have questioned. A warning failed to reach the person who needed it. An uncertain prediction appeared more authoritative than it really was. A decision-maker misunderstood what a model could do. A worker noticed something was wrong but did not have the institutional authority to stop deployment. A system technically disclosed its limitations, but in a way nobody could reasonably use.
From where I sit, these do not look like conventional model failures. They look like communication failures. Thus, I have come to an alternate viewpoint that AI risk is also a communication problem. This is not to say that technical risk does not matter. But AI systems do not produce consequences by themselves. Their outputs enter relationships among people, organizations, institutions, and other technologies. Somewhere between what a system produces and what eventually happens, information has to be interpreted, trusted, contested, communicated, ignored, escalated, or acted upon. In those in betweens, risk abounds.

title: AI Risk Is a Communication Problem
section: A model output is not yet a social consequence
text:
A model output is not yet a social consequence
Imagine that an AI system produces an incorrect answer. At the model level, we might call this a hallucination, and hallucination at that point is not yet a social problem. It becomes a social problem only when someone encounters it and interprets it in a way that produces consequences. They may trust it, reject it, verify it, misunderstand it, forward it to someone else, use it to make a decision, or feed it into another system.
The same incorrect output could therefore disappear without consequence in one setting and produce substantial harm in another. But if the model output stays largely the same with varying outcomes, then something outside the model is doing important causal work.
Communication is part of that process.
This is one reason I find the sociotechnical framing of AI risk so integral. In their paper “Concrete Problems in AI Safety”, Dario Amodei et al identified problems like avoiding negative side effects, reward hacking, scalable supervision, safe exploration, and robustness to distributional shift. The paper became foundational partly because it helped interpret broad concerns about AI safety into concrete technical research problems.
But once AI systems leave experimental settings and enter workplaces, hospitals, schools, government agencies, financial institutions, newsrooms, and homes, technical properties interact with social ones. So beyond whether the system fails technically, we also have to ask whether anyone recognizes the failure as a failure.

title: AI Risk Is a Communication Problem
text:
Uncertainty has to be communicated
AI systems are probabilistic, but the interfaces through which we encounter them often do not feel probabilistic at all. A chatbot does not usually look uncertain. It gives you an answer, good ones, I must add, sometimes, even an excellent one, and sometimes an answer that is completely wrong with exactly the same confidence, fluency, and grammatical composure.
This creates an unusual communication problem. Humans use communicative cues to evaluate other humans all the time. Hesitation tells us something, so does qualification. “I think” means something different from “I know.” A physician saying “the evidence is unclear” communicates something different from one saying “your test confirms this.” Generative AI complicates those cues because linguistic confidence and epistemic confidence are not the same thing.
The system can sound certain without possessing anything equivalent to human certainty.
I read this research on automation which warned about related problems for decades. Raja Parasuraman and Victor Riley’s classic paper, “Humans and Automation: Use, Misuse, Disuse, Abuse”, showed that the relationship between people and automated systems cannot be understood simply by asking whether automation works. People can over-rely on it, underuse it, or use it in ways its designers did not anticipate.
AI intensifies this problem because many contemporary systems communicate through language. The interface can be persuasive, can sound like a human, an expert or a friend. It can sound like a doctor, lawyer, or journalist. It can sound like someone who knows what they are talking about even when they do not. So, just maybe, one AI risk question should be: Does the system communicate what it knows, what it does not know, and when that difference is important
That is partly an engineering problem, but it is unmistakably a communication problem too.

title: AI Risk Is a Communication Problem
section: Transparency is useless if nobody understands it
text:
Transparency is useless if nobody understands it
Our default response to these concerns is usually asking for transparency. Disclose that AI was used, publish a model card, document the training process, explain the limitations, provide confidence scores, add a warning.
I support many of these interventions, but I think we sometimes confuse making information available with communicating. They are not the same thing.
A forty-page technical document sitting on a website is technically transparent. Same goes for a model card that only an ML engineer can interpret, a disclaimer that users click through without reading, or a confidence score that a decision-maker does not understand. The information exists, but that does not mean it has successfully communicated anything.
This brings to mind the works of Timnit Gebruet al on “Datasheets for Datasets”, and Margaret Mitchell et al on “Model Cards for Model Reporting”. Both interventions recognized that responsible AI development requires information to travel across boundaries. Dataset creators, therefore, need to communicate information to dataset users, and so does model developers need to communicate intended uses, performance characteristics, limitations, and evaluation conditions to people who did not build the system.
I think their importance go beyond documentation, as it also highlight that in AI governance, Responsibility depends on successful information transfer. Because if someone knows something about the system, someone else needs to know it. But it is the structure connecting those two people determines whether that knowledge becomes actionable.

title: AI Risk Is a Communication Problem
section: The person who knows about the risk may not be the person who can stop it
text:
The person who knows about the risk may not be the person who can stop it
This one is more apparent inside organizations. Imagine an engineer finds out a serious limitation in an AI system scheduled for deployment. What happens next?
Technically, the risk has been identified, but organizationally, almost nothing has happened yet. So, the engineer has to communicate it, and someone has to believe them. In the typical setting, the issue has to move through whatever reporting structure exists. A manager may have to escalate it, and the product team may disagree on its severity, legal may see things differently, while leadership may have commercial incentives to proceed. So, at the end of the day, someone eventually has to possess both enough information to understand the problem and enough authority to act on it.
This is where I think some discussions of AI governance is too fixated on principles and not enough on communication structures. An organization can have excellent AI principles and still be unsafe if bad news does not travel upward. It can have, say, a responsible AI team whose recommendations arrive after product decisions have effectively been made; or a technically sophisticated evaluators whose findings are put across in a dashboard that senior decision-makers barely understand. More generally, it can have a culture in which people are afraid to raise concerns, or even the ones who do are ignored. So you see, the problem is not that nobody knew about the risk, the problem is that the knowledge could not move to the right person at the right time.

title: AI Risk Is a Communication Problem
section: Risk communication has been studying this problem for a long time
text:
Risk communication has been studying this problem for a long time
I believe this is also where AI research can learn from fields that have spent decades studying how people understand hazards. The way people perceive risk, how they respond to uncertainty, and how organizations communicate hazards has been studied in public health, environmental communication, disaster communication, nuclear safety, and other areas. It did not begin with artificial intelligence.
Paul Slovic’s work on “Perception of Risk” showed that public perceptions of risk do not simply mirror technical probability calculations. People respond to characteristics such as unfamiliarity, controllability, catastrophic potential, and dread. This is quite similar to artificial intelligence, and like, I mentioned earlier, different groups may encounter different dimensions of the same technology. Those experiences are sometimes described as misunderstanding, which I am unsure of, regardless, communication is how those understandings meet or fail to.

title: AI Risk Is a Communication Problem
section: We need to talk about who can be believed
text:
We need to talk about who can be believed
Communication is also about power. It is about who can speak, who can be heard, and who can be believed. In this kind of conversation, communication rarely occurs between equally positioned people. Who can raise an AI risk, whose assessment is valued, and who gets dismissed as technically uninformed, who has access to the information needed to challenge a system, and who can demand an explanation, and who has enough institutional authority to stop deployment are all questions of power.
All users of a system may encounter different aspects of its failures, but knowledge is knowledge, and power is power (thank you Cersei Lannister). Therefore, communication should not be treated as a final step in AI risk management, for communication is part of how risk becomes known from the get go

title: AI Risk Is a Communication Problem
text:
Human oversight depends on communication
We hear all the time that humans should remain “in the loop.” This one, I have a controversial take on (coming soon).
Putting a human somewhere in an automated process does not tell us very much. Starting off, what does the human see? What information does the system provide? Can the human understand why the system produced its recommendation? How much time do they have to intervene? Can they override it? What happens when they disagree? Does disagreement carry a professional cost? Does the system communicate its limbo in a form the human can actually interpret?
Take it or leave it, but I think the human-in-the-loop framing is often a red herring. It is not the presence of a human that matters, it is the quality of the interaction between the human and the system. A human who cannot understand, challenge, or meaningfully alter an automated decision is not providing much oversight.
Permit me to tap into the work of Madeleine Elish on “Moral Crumple Zones” who describes situations in which humans positioned around complex automated systems can absorb responsibility when those systems fail, even when meaningful control was distributed much more broadly.
As a communication scholar, I see a communication dimension to this too. For if we want humans to provide oversight, we have to design the informational relationship between humans and machines in ways that make oversight possible. Human oversight is not a person, it is a relationship.

title: AI Risk Is a Communication Problem
section: AI risk also travels between organizations
text:
AI risk also travels between organizations
Take some time to imagine how AI systems become embedded in larger technical ecosystems. One company develops a foundation model, another company builds an application on top of it, and a third organization deploys that application. Employees use it to make decisions involving customers, and customers experience the consequences.
Now imagine a vulnerability, bias, data problem, or reliability issue surges up upstream. Who needs to know? How quickly? In what language? With what level of technical detail? Who is responsible for informing downstream users? How do downstream organizations determine whether the issue affects their particular implementation? What happens when the system is updated? So AI supply chains are also communication chains.
This becomes especially important as we move toward increasingly agentic systems in which one model’s output can become another system’s input. A misleading output may not need a human to act on it before producing consequences. Here, machines can communicate with machines without human intervention. Agents can call tools, retrieve information, update databases, trigger workflows, and pass generated information to other agents. Even so, the communication problem is still there even when the human leaves the interaction. It only becomes more complicated.

title: AI Risk Is a Communication Problem
section: The Global South makes this more complicated
text:
The Global South makes this more complicated
Lets talk about borders. Many of the most serious AI risks are technical and also social, institutional, and political. The contextual risks of AI systems vary across countries, cultures, and institutions. For example, a system may be considered sufficiently accurate globally while performing poorly for languages or populations poorly represented in its training and evaluation data, it could be safe in one country but not in another because of differences in regulatory regimes, institutional capacity, or cultural norms.
So beyond responding to AI risk from by clamouring for better universal standards, we also have to ask whether risk information survives translation across technical, linguistic, institutional, and cultural boundaries. A safety warning produced in San Francisco does not automatically become meaningful governance in Onitsha or Aba simply because someone published it online.
As information travel, meaning travel with it, and sometimes it does not.

title: AI Risk Is a Communication Problem
section: Maybe AI literacy is not enough
text:
Maybe AI literacy is not enough
Another common answer to these problems is AI literacy. The assumption is that if we teach people how AI works, to not trust everything a chatbot says, to recognize hallucinations, they will be able to interpret its outputs, recognize its limitations, and understand its risks. Again, a very useful idea. I support it. I have taught AI literacy myself, and I think it is useful. But it is rather confining to make literacy our primary solution.
At some point, we may default to transferring responsibility from systems and institutions to users. If an AI system routinely communicates its limitations badly, the answer cannot simply be to train millions of people to become better interpreters of unclear or unreliable outputs. If an organization deploys a complex automated system without meaningful ways for people to challenge its decisions, simply educating users about algorithms is not an adequate solution. Literacy matters, so does design, institutional structure, and power.
Responsibility has to travel in more than one direction.

title: AI Risk Is a Communication Problem
section: I think communication scholars belong in this conversation
text:
I think communication scholars belong in this conversation
AI risk has understandably been shaped by computer science, as many of the problems require technical expertise. Security vulnerabilities need technical solutions. Models need rigorous evaluations. Robustness needs to be measured. Dangerous capabilities need to be understood.
My stake here is not to replace any of that with communication theory, but to explore what happens when we acknowledge that technical evaluation cannot tell us everything about whether an AI system will be safe in the world. Because the moment an AI system encounters a person, a team, an organization, or an institution, communication begins doing causal work. People form expectations about the system, interpret outputs, they make decisions, they escalate concerns, they ignore warnings, they trust or distrust systems. Publics communicate back through resistance, adoption, reinterpretation, and demands for accountability. Communication is not a side effect of AI risk, but a part of the infrastructure through which AI risk becomes socially consequential.

title: AI Risk Is a Communication Problem
section: So what would it mean to take communication seriously?
text:
So what would it mean to take communication seriously?
Perhaps AI evaluation would go beyond whether a model knows the right answer to whether it appropriately communicates when it does not. Or maybe red teaming would test both dangerous outputs and how people interpret those outputs. Perhaps model documentation would be evaluated with the people (or at least a representative sample of them) expected to use it. That organizations would evaluate whether risk information can actually go from technical teams to decision-makers. Maybe human oversight would be evaluated as an interaction and not just confirmed by the presence of a human somewhere in a workflow. Or that incident reporting would examine who knew what, when they knew it, whom they told, and where the information stopped moving. That global AI governance would expand focus from the existence of standards to how their meaning survives across institutional and cultural contexts. And perhaps communication researchers would stop researching AI primarily as another technology people talk about and begin examining communication as part of the safety architecture. I am especially excited about the last one.

title: AI Risk Is a Communication Problem
section: The risk is not only in the model
text:
The risk is not only in the model
I am not saying that every AI problem can be solved through better communication. A dnagerous model is a dangerous model. A security vulnerability, bias, or discriminatory system require more than better messaging. Some systems should not be deployed at all. But technical risk and communication risk are greatly intertwined.
A system can fail technically and recover because people recognize the problem quickly and have the information and authority to intervene; while a system can be technically sound and still produce catastrophic consequences because people misinterpret its outputs, ignore warnings, or fail to escalate concerns.So maybe the focus should go beyond asking How risky is this AI system? to also asking What happens to information about risk once this system enters the world? Who sees it? Who understands or believes it? Who can communicate or challenge it? And, ultimately, who has the power to do something about it?
AI risk is a technical problem, it is an organizational problem, it is an institutional problem, and it is a political problem. And much more than we currently acknowledge, AI risk is a communication problem.

title: Journalism After Generative AI
section: I have thought a lot about what is left…?
text:
I have thought a lot about what is left…?
Before I became a researcher studying artificial intelligence, I was a journalist, and I spent years reporting, writing, and editing news stories in Nigeria. I have also spent years studying how journalists work with technology, including AI. Maybe, just maybe, that is why I find some of the conversations about generative AI and journalism somewhat fragmented.
A lot of our attention has been on whether AI will replace journalists and I get it. Journalism has already lived through decades of shrinking newsrooms, declining advertising revenue, platform dependence, and changing audience habits. A technology that can summarize documents, transcribe interviews, suggest headlines, rewrite copy, generate images, search large collections of text, and produce something resembling a news story in seconds understandably raises questions about what is left for the journalists to do.
But, let us take some moment and think about a different question.
What is left of journalism when more of the work of journalism can be automated?
Can we think beyond whether journalists will still have jobs? Because journalism has never been about just text production. A journalist decides whom to call and whom not to call, what stories to be skeptical about, which detail changes the meaning of a story, whether a source knows what they claim to know, when two technically accurate statements create a misleading impression when placed together, and whether something should be published just because it can be verified.
These decisions are so embedded in everyday newsroom work that we sometimes talk about them just as judgment. Generative AI is entering that process, and I think that repositions things considerably.

title: Journalism After Generative AI
section: AI did not just crash into journalism
text:
AI did not just crash into journalism
A trip down memory lane reminds us that journalism’s relationship with artificial intelligence did not begin with ChatGPT. News organizations have used automation for years to produce earnings reports, sports stories, election results, recommendation systems, transcription, translation, content moderation, and other forms of computational journalism. What changed with generative AI is partly the range of activities that can now be automated, thus moving the technology much closer to the intellectual center of journalistic work.
A global JournalismAI survey by Charlie Beckett and Mira Yaseen, “Generating Change”, surveyed 105 news organizations across 46 countries and found widespread experimentation with AI across newsgathering, production, and distribution. Nearly three-quarters of the organizations surveyed believed generative AI presented new opportunities for journalism. (LSE). The optimism checks out, because a reporter can use AI to work through a long government document, generate possible interview questions, transcribe an hour-long conversation, translate material, summarize background information, restructure notes, or identify patterns in a dataset.
For journalists working under constant deadline pressure, these are not trivial conveniences. If my memory serves me right, in the newsroom work, there was always another story, you know, something that needs to go out, information that still needs to be confirmed while the clock keeps moving. So when a technology promises to give journalists some of that time back, I understand the attraction.
A few years ago, I interviewed 18 Nigerian journalists for what eventually became my study, “Journalists’ Perception of Artificial Intelligence: The Case of Nigerian Newsrooms”, published in Digital Journalism. I wanted to understand how journalists were making sense of AI as it entered their work, and also whether geography and culture changed that encounter.
The journalists I interviewed saw clear benefits in using AI, particularly for creativity and efficiency, but they also worried about what I described as intellectual dormancy. Which is the possibility that increasing reliance on AI could weaken some of the intellectual effort journalists bring to their work. They also raised a related concern that I think is important here, that is, that AI-generated content lack the journalistic values that ordinarily shape how information becomes news.
Again, the bigger concern is what are we trading on the altar of convenience?

title: Journalism After Generative AI
section: Verification becomes more important as production becomes easier
text:
Verification becomes more important as production becomes easier
There is also an uncomfortable contradiction at the center of generative AI and journalism. Think about it. We have developed machines that can produce plausible information extraordinarily quickly at exactly the moment when determining whether information is trustworthy has become extraordinarily difficult.
A language model can produce a clean summary of a complicated document. But keep in mind that clean is not the same thing as correct. In the process of producing that clean summary, the model can collapse nuance, uncertainty, and ambiguity. It can omit inconvenient details, produce a misleading connection, or generate a citation that looks real but does not actually exist. It can produce something that looks like journalism without actually being journalism.
For most professions, these are reliability problems. For journalism, they are existential problems, for they touch the very reason journalism exists. Journalism is not just about producing information, can the produced information be trusted?
Verification is one of the practices through which journalism distinguishes itself from the enormous amount of information circulating around it. Generative AI therefore creates an interesting reversal. The easier it becomes to produce information, the more valuable this difficult work of verifying information becomes. And yet verification is exactly the part that is not conveniently fast.
So, if AI summarizes twenty documents for me, I still need some way of knowing that the summary accurately represents those documents. If it translates an interview, someone needs to know whether the translation preserved what the source actually meant with appropriate context. If it suggests that two events are connected, a journalist still has to establish whether that relationship exists.
At some point, a human being has to decide that I am willing to put my name, or my newsroom’s name, behind this. This is exactly the point at which judgment becomes consequential. It is not enough to say that a journalist clicked “approve” at the end of an automated workflow, because, the journalist must have enough knowledge of the material to know whether it is accurate, fair, and trustworthy. This decision cannot be another output in the pipeline or one outsourced to a machine. It is also not something that can be done without understanding the material, the context, and the implications of publishing it.

title: Journalism After Generative AI
section: The journalist is becoming an editor of machine output
text:
The journalist is becoming an editor of machine output
Generative AI does not have to replace journalists to transform the profession, it only has to redistribute what journalists spend their time doing.
For the journalistic work, I think we are seeing a shift in what journalists do. The journalist is increasingly becoming an editor of machine output. The journalist is not just producing information, they are supervising, selecting, correcting, verifying, and approving the work of a machine.
A recent study by Chang Sup Park and Temitope Akintade “Artificial intelligence in Nigerian newsrooms: Navigating jurisdictional hybridization, retreat, and maintenance”, where they interviewed 50 journalists in Nigerian newsrooms and examined AI through the question of professional jurisdiction: essentially, what work belongs to journalists and what happens when technology begins doing some of it. They found AI being used for activities including transcription, copyediting, and preliminary drafting, producing different configurations in which journalists maintain, share, or retreat from areas of professional work. (SAGE)
I want to nitpick a little on the idea of jurisdiction here because it gets us beyond the dramatic question of replacement. Professions are partly defined by the tasks over which they claim expertise. So what happens when those tasks begin moving? Think about it for a moment. If a journalist no longer transcribes the interview, writes the first draft, develops the headline, summarizes the background documents, or rewrites the copy, perhaps the journalist’s role increasingly shifts toward supervising, selecting, correcting, verifying, and approving.
That does not necessarily make the journalist less important. But we have to objectively see that it does make the journalist different. And I am not sure we have fully considered what that difference means for the field of journalism, for the public, and for the journalists themselves.

title: Journalism After Generative AI
section: There are things I learned by doing the “inefficient” work
text:
There are things I learned by doing the “inefficient” work
SOmetimes, I too, am uncomfortable with the language of efficiency. Some newsroom tasks are genuinely tedious, and I do not think anyone needs to romanticize them. But some of the work that is often described as inefficient is also where journalists learn what they need to know to make good decisions.
Listening to an interview again while transcribing it may mean hearing the hesitation you missed the first time. Reading a long report yourself may mean noticing the paragraph that would never survive an automated summary but changes how you understand the document. Writing a bad first draft forces you to discover that you do not yet understand your own story.
Even rewriting can be epistemic work, because you are not just rearranging sentences, for the fun of it, you are deciding what really happened.
If generative AI increasingly performs the intermediate work between gathering information and producing a finished story, journalists may become more efficient while simultaneously becoming more removed from the material from which their judgment is supposed to emerge.
I am not saying that we should return to typewriters and handwritten notebooks o. I am saying that efficiency cannot be the only measure of successful AI integration. We should also ask what journalists learn through the work being automated.

title: Journalism After Generative AI
section: And then there is the Global South
text:
And then there is the Global South
Let us make a slight detour from the best-resourced newsrooms. Gregory Gondwe’s study, “CHATGPT and the Global South: How are journalists in sub-Saharan Africa engaging with generative AI?”, interviewed journalists across several sub-Saharan African countries and found both enthusiasm and serious concern around generative AI. Journalists were navigating questions of misinformation, plagiarism, stereotypes, and the poor representation of African contexts within the data underlying these systems. (De Gruyter)
We must keep in mind that the same tool does not enter every newsroom under the same conditions. Imagine two journalists using the same generative AI system. One works in a large newsroom with dedicated technology staff, legal counsel, an AI policy, paid access to several tools, editors trained to recognize AI-related failures, and enough institutional resources to experiment carefully. The other works in an understaffed newsroom where reporters already perform several roles, institutional AI guidelines barely exist, access to premium tools is limited, internet infrastructure is inconsistent, and the languages and local realities being reported are poorly represented in the systems. They are technically using the same technology, but they are not experiencing the same technological transition.
Allen Munoriyarwa’s research on Southern African newsrooms makes this point particularly well. His study of AI integration across newsrooms in South Africa, Lesotho, Eswatini, Botswana, and Zimbabwe identifies barriers that are simultaneously social and technological. AI adoption is shaped not just by whether tools exist, but by infrastructure, organizational resources, professional practices, and the environments in which journalists actually work. (SAGE)
So, admittedly, I am wary of universal predictions about the “AI newsroom.” There is no single newsroom into which AI is arriving. There are many newsrooms, each with different resources, practices, and constraints. The same technology can have very different implications depending on the context in which it is used.

title: Journalism After Generative AI
section: In some places, AI may fill gaps before it replaces jobs
text:
In some places, AI may fill gaps before it replaces jobs
Hear me out.
Much of the anxiety around AI and journalism assumes that this automation enters an existing role and removes the human performing it. But what happens in newsrooms where that human role barely exists?
A newsroom may need a data journalist but cannot afford one, or transcription services but reporters transcribe their own interviews. It may want to translate stories into several local languages but lack the staff to do so, or someone monitoring thousands of government documents but have three reporters covering an entire beat. In these environments, AI may not initially replace existing capacity, but instead provide capacity that was never there to begin with.
So we have to agree that valuable contributions come from this integration, ones that might not have been possible otherwise. But it also introduces another dependency. If resource-constrained newsrooms become dependent on AI systems developed elsewhere, trained primarily on data from elsewhere, priced by companies elsewhere, and governed through infrastructures they do not control, then automation may solve one inequality while deepening another.
This is one reason I think the political economy of newsroom AI deserves far more attention. We should not only ask whether journalists have access to AI, we should ask what kind of access they have, under whose terms, and what happens when that access becomes essential to producing news.

title: Journalism After Generative AI
text:
What happens to professional identity?
This one is personal.
Journalists develop identities around what they know how to do. You learn how to interview, to write quickly, to edit, to verify, to investigate, to report. You learn how to ask questions that are not answered in the first paragraph of a press release. You learn how to recognize when someone is avoiding your question. You learn that the apparently insignificant sentence in a document is sometimes the story. You learn what your editor will send back. You learn how to write a story,a headline, and a lede that is accurate and compelling.
Eventually, these things become part of what it means to say, I am a journalist. So I wonder what happens when some of those competencies are increasingly shared with machines. Maybe journalistic identity moves upward toward judgment. Or, maybe, the better journalist is no longer the one who can produce 800 words quickly, but the person who knows whether those 800 words deserve to even exist.
Perhaps verification, source relationships, contextual knowledge, ethical reasoning, investigation, and editorial judgment become more central because writing becomes cheaper. I find something hopeful in that possibility, because Generative AI might force journalism to become clearer about what journalism contributes that text generation does not.

title: Journalism After Generative AI
text:
Judgment cannot become a slogan
But seriously!
It is easy to respond to every concern about newsroom automation by saying that humans will retain editorial judgment. Reassuring right? But not particularly helpful. It is like saying that humans will always be in charge of airplanes, even as autopilot systems increasingly fly them. It is true, but it does not tell us much about what that actually means.
Judgment is not something a journalist simply possesses by virtue of being human. This judgment is developed through experience, through making mistakes, through reporting, editing, learning a beat, understanding communities, being corrected by people who know more than you do, and doing many of the mundane tasks that automation now promises to remove.
If entry-level journalists increasingly begin their careers supervising AI-generated material instead of developing stories from the ground up, where will the next generation of editorial judgment come from? I find this question way more interesting than whether AI can write a convincing news article.
Beyond asking which tasks AI can perform, can we spare time to ask which professional capabilities humans develop while performing those tasks. Because if we automate the task, we need to know whether we are also interrupting the process through which expertise is produced.

title: Journalism After Generative AI
section: The audience is also in the room
text:
The audience is also in the room
And then there is trust.
News organizations are introducing generative AI during a period when public trust in news is already fragile. Newsrooms may see AI primarily as an internal production technology, while the audience may see something else entirely.
Was this written by a journalist? Was this image real? Did someone check the facts? Was the interview conducted by a person? Did an editor read this before I did? These questions are becoming part of the audience’s encounter with news whether journalists want them to be or not. This is where transparency comes in, but even disclosure alone does not solve the problem. A small label saying “AI assisted” tells me that AI was involved, but it does not tell me what it did.
There is a huge difference between using AI to transcribe a recorded interview and asking it to generate the first version of an investigative story. There is a difference between translation and verification, between using AI to search a document collection and allowing it to determine what claims appear in the published story.
Maybe news organizations will eventually need a much richer vocabulary for describing human-machine collaboration. This is not because audiences need a technical report attached to every article. It is because trust depends partly on understanding how knowledge was produced.

title: Journalism After Generative AI
section: Maybe the future journalist is not competing with AI
text:
Maybe the future journalist is not competing with AI
I particularly do not find the question Will AI replace journalists? useful. It is too large to tell us much.
Of course, some jobs may disappear. Some tasks almost certainly will. Others will become more valuable. Entirely new forms of journalistic work may spring up. But I think that the more interesting transformation is happening inside the occupation. Consider what journalists do, what they know, and what they are expected to verify. Consider which decisions are still theirs, which decisions sip into technical systems, and which skills stop we no longer need to learn because a machine performs the work first.
This is why I think the future of journalism will be less dependent on mapping a clear boundary between human journalism and artificial intelligence. The boundary is already becoming difficult to maintain. The harder work, and probably, the most important one is deciding where human judgment must remain consequential. I do not mean consequential in the sense of ceremonial like clicking “approve” at the end of an automated workflow. CON-SE-QUEN-TIAL.

title: Journalism After Generative AI
text:
Journalism after generative AI
I am not nostalgic for a version of journalism untouched by technology, no such version has ever existed.
Journalists have always worked through technologies ranging from notebooks, telephones, cameras, recorders, databases, search engines, content management systems, social media, analytics platforms, and now generative AI. Each changed what journalists could do, and some changed what journalism became.
Unlike previous technologies, generative AI feels different because it does not just help journalists transmit, record, retrieve, or distribute information. It increasingly participates in interpreting and producing news work. And that puts the technology unusually close to the epistemic heart of journalism.
The future of journalism will not be secured just by keeping humans somewhere in the workflow. It will depend on preserving the conditions under which journalists can still know what they are publishing, understand why they believe it, challenge the systems assisting them, and take responsibility for the decisions made along the way.
Especially in the Global South, that future cannot be designed around an imaginary universal newsroom with unlimited tools, stable infrastructure, abundant staff, and well-resourced verification systems. It has to begin with the newsrooms that actually exist.
I still believe generative AI can make journalism better, but I think that the real measure of that success will not be how much faster journalists can produce news. It will be whether, after all that automation, they are still capable of telling us why we should believe it.

text:
Ph.D. Researcher — Temple University


Amaka Peace Onebunne


Sociotechnical Systems Researcher


Temple University · Philadelphia, Pennsylvania


I study the relationships among people, emerging technologies, organizations, institutions, and society, with much of my current work centered on artificial intelligence. I look at how these technologies become part of communication, professional practice, decision-making, and everyday social and organizational life. Questions of human–machine interaction, trust, evaluation, information integrity, knowledge, and sociotechnical systems run across this work, including the growing presence of machines within shared social and information environments.
My work brings together computational social science, experiments, human studies, media, and communication theories. Africa and the Global South are also important sites for my research, especially for understanding how technologies travel and also carry particular visions of the technological future across contexts, whose experiences and assumptions shape them, and how different societies encounter and shape technological change.
